headline: World leaders gather at a deeply divided UN

sources.title: War, runaway AI and climate shocks to take center stage as world leaders meet at UN (Associated Press, via ABC7 New York)
What to know as world leaders converge at the United Nations this week (NPR, via OPB)
Guterres: 'Cracks have become canyons' as world faces four tests of power (UN News)

chunks.text: World leaders {{came together}} in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly. The main debate {{kicked off}} on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. About 130 [[heads of state]] and government are expected to speak. The meeting takes place amid wars and [[bitter divisions]]. Russia's president is not attending. India's prime minister {{backed out}}. China's president sent a vice president instead.

verbs.correct: To meet in one place as a group
verbs.why: Our whole family comes together for dinner on Thanksgiving, and neighbors often come together for a town meeting. World leaders came together in New York this week for the UN General Assembly.

verbs.correct: To start, as an event does
verbs.wrong: To relax after a busy time
verbs.why: The festival kicks off with a parade on Friday, and the season kicks off in early September. The main debate at the UN kicked off on Tuesday, September 22, 2026.

verbs.correct: To decide not to do what was planned
verbs.why: Two players backed out of the game at the last minute, and the buyer backed out of the deal. India's prime minister backed out of the trip to New York.

chunks.text: The UN secretary-general opened the debate with his final speech. "Cracks have become [[canyons]]," he said. He {{set out}} four tests: war or peace, [[inequality]], climate change, and artificial intelligence. Wars are still {{going on}} in Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, and other places. The war in Ukraine is in its fifth year. Ukraine and its European [[allies]] are seeking more support. Russia has used its Security Council [[veto]] to block UN [[involvement]]. He also {{spoke out}} against machines making [[life-and-death decisions]].

verbs.correct: To explain ideas in a clear order
verbs.wrong: To start a new group or company
verbs.why: The coach set out the plan for the new season, and the report sets out three main goals. The UN chief set out four tests for the world, including war or peace and climate change.
The noise went on all night, and the meeting went on for hours. Wars are still going on in Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, and other places.

verbs.correct: To state strongly in public what you oppose
verbs.wrong: To talk officially on behalf of others
verbs.why: Many doctors have spoken out against smoking in parks, and a few students spoke out against the new rule. The UN chief spoke out against machines making life-and-death decisions.

chunks.text: The UN is also [[short of money]]. The United States paid $725 million of its [[dues]] this year, so it kept its vote in the Assembly. An expert at the International Crisis Group said money troubles forced the UN to {{cut back on}} [[peacekeeping]] and [[humanitarian aid]]. [[Supply chain]] problems are {{pushing up}} [[living costs]]. They are also {{slowing down}} growth. The secretary-general said [[cooperation]] is more necessary than ever to {{deal with}} the world's biggest threats.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To interrupt someone who is talking
verbs.why: The school had to cut back on sports when its budget fell, and many families cut back on eating out. Money troubles forced the UN to cut back on peacekeeping and humanitarian aid.

verbs.correct: To make a price or cost rise
verbs.wrong: To delay something to a later time
verbs.why: A poor harvest can push up the price of bread, and high demand pushes up rents in big cities. Supply chain problems are pushing up living costs around the world.

verbs.correct: To make something happen less quickly
verbs.wrong: To close a business or system completely
verbs.why: Heavy snow slowed down the delivery of mail, and a weak market can slow down hiring. Supply chain problems are also slowing down economic growth.

verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem
verbs.wrong: To buy and sell a type of goods
verbs.why: The city hired more workers to deal with the trash problem, and the school met with parents to deal with bullying. The UN chief said cooperation is more necessary than ever to deal with the world's biggest threats.

chunks.text: The secretary-general's second five-year [[term]] ends on December 31. The Security Council has held three [[straw polls]] but has not {{settled on}} anyone to {{take over}} from him. By tradition, the next leader is expected to come from Latin America. A former president of Chile {{dropped out}} over the weekend, leaving seven [[candidates]]. No woman has ever held the job, and many countries want that to change. The United States says the next leader must get the UN "back to basics."

verbs.correct: To finally choose one after discussion
verbs.wrong: To get used to a new home or job
verbs.why: After a long talk, we settled on a name for the dog, and the team settled on blue for its new jerseys. The Security Council has held three straw polls but has not settled on anyone to replace the UN chief.

verbs.correct: To take someone's job after they leave
verbs.wrong: To hire new workers for a business
verbs.why: A new manager will take over when the owner retires, and her deputy took over when she left. No one has yet been chosen to take over from the UN chief when his term ends on December 31.

verbs.correct: To leave a contest before it ends
verbs.wrong: To visit someone without a plan
verbs.why: Two runners dropped out of the race after ten miles, and one candidate dropped out of the election in March. A former president of Chile dropped out of the race for secretary-general over the weekend, leaving seven candidates.

mainIdea.s: World leaders met at the UN amid wars, money troubles and deep disagreements. In his last speech there, the UN chief named four big tests, and no successor has been chosen yet.
mainIdea.why: Leaders came together amid wars and bitter divisions, and the secretary-general set out four tests. The Security Council has not settled on anyone to replace him.

mainIdea.s: The yearly Assembly opened with conflicts and budget problems high on the agenda. Its outgoing leader used his final address to announce that a woman from Latin America will succeed him.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no successor has been chosen. The Security Council has held three straw polls without agreement, and seven candidates are still in the race.

mainIdea.s: The Security Council held an emergency session after a new border war broke out. Members voted to send thousands of extra peacekeepers and to double the budget for their mission.
mainIdea.why: There was no emergency session or vote on peacekeepers. Money troubles have actually forced the UN to cut back on peacekeeping.

tf.s: India's prime minister backed out of the trip to New York.
tf.why: He backed out of the trip, while Russia's president is not attending and China's president sent a vice president.

tf.s: The UN chief set out four tests, including climate change.
tf.why: He set out four tests for the world: war or peace, inequality, climate change, and artificial intelligence.

tf.s: The United States paid no dues to the UN this year.
tf.why: It paid $725 million of its dues, but the UN still had to cut back on peacekeeping and aid because of money troubles.

tf.s: The Security Council has settled on a woman to lead the UN.
tf.why: After three straw polls, it has not settled on anyone to take over, and seven candidates remain.

tf.s: Supply chain problems are pushing up living costs.
tf.why: These problems are pushing up living costs and also slowing down economic growth.

lines.text: Did you follow the UN meeting in New York this week?
A little. Lots of leaders {{came together}}, didn't they?
Yes, but India's prime minister {{backed out}}. Russia's president isn't coming, and China sent a vice president.
That's a lot of [[empty chairs]]. How did it start?
The debate {{kicked off}} on Tuesday with the secretary-general's last speech. He said the cracks in the world have become canyons.
Strong words. What did he talk about?
He {{set out}} four tests: war or peace, inequality, climate change, and AI. He also {{spoke out}} against machines making life-and-death decisions.
And the wars are still {{going on}} in Ukraine, Sudan, and other places. [[No shortage of trouble]].
The UN is short of money, too. It had to {{cut back on}} peacekeeping and aid.
Didn't the United States pay its dues?
It paid $725 million this year. Still, the UN is struggling just to [[keep the lights on]].
Meanwhile, prices keep rising at home.
Supply chain problems are {{pushing up}} living costs and {{slowing down}} growth. He says countries have to work together to {{deal with}} big threats like these.
So who will {{take over}} when he leaves in December?
Nobody knows. The Security Council hasn't {{settled on}} anyone, and one candidate {{dropped out}} last weekend.
It could go [[down to the wire]].
Many countries want a woman this time. No woman has ever held the job.
Then maybe a woman will finally [[break the glass ceiling]] at the UN.

expressions.def: Used to point out that important people did not come to an event
ex: Half the board skipped the meeting. That's a lot of empty chairs.
The ceremony had some empty chairs where the stars should have been.

expressions.def: Used to say there are many problems at the same time
ex: The roof leaks and the car won't start. No shortage of trouble this week.
New job, new city, sick kids. No shortage of trouble.

expressions.def: To have just enough money to keep an organization running
ex: The small theater sells snacks to keep the lights on.
Donations barely keep the lights on at the shelter.

expressions.def: Used to say a decision or contest will not be settled until the very last moment
ex: The election went down to the wire.
With one day left, the deal is going down to the wire.

expressions.def: To be the first woman or member of a group to reach a high position
ex: She broke the glass ceiling when she became the company's first female CEO.
Many hoped the vote would break the glass ceiling.
